clinicalPearls: A rare autosomal recessive glycolytic enzymopathy causing chronic non-spherocytic, Coombs-negative haemolytic anaemia
Because hexokinase catalyses the first, rate-limiting step of glycolysis, deficiency can produce clinically significant anaemia even with modest reductions in activity
Presentation is often in the neonatal period or infancy with jaundice and anaemia
Unlike pyruvate kinase deficiency, red-cell 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate tends to be low rather than high, subtly shifting the oxygen dissociation curve
Some patients have a multisystem phenotype, including HK1-related conditions affecting other tissues, reflecting the gene's broad expression
Diagnosis is by reduced red-cell hexokinase activity on assay, interpreted with care because activity is high in young reticulocytes, and HK1 mutation testing
Management is supportive with folate, transfusion when required and splenectomy considered in severe transfusion-dependent disease
reference.pathophysiology: Hexokinase phosphorylates glucose to glucose-6-phosphate, committing it to glycolysis, the mature red cell's sole source of ATP. As the enzyme catalyses the first and rate-limiting step, reduced activity throttles the whole pathway, lowering ATP production and shortening red-cell survival to cause a chronic non-spherocytic haemolytic anaemia. Because hexokinase activity is normally highest in young red cells and declines with cell age, the reticulocytosis of haemolysis can partly mask the deficiency on assay, requiring age-adjusted interpretation.
additionalInvestigations: Red-cell hexokinase enzyme assay with reticulocyte-age adjustment
Full blood count, reticulocyte count and blood film
Haemolysis screen with bilirubin, lactate dehydrogenase and haptoglobin
Direct antiglobulin test to exclude immune haemolysis
Molecular testing of the HK1 gene
redFlags: Severe neonatal jaundice risking kernicterus and requiring exchange transfusion
Aplastic crisis following parvovirus B19 infection
Symptoms of impaired oxygen delivery from a leftward-shifted dissociation curve
reference.prognosis: Most patients have a chronic compensated or transfusion-supported anaemia; severity depends on residual enzyme activity, and the low 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate may make a given haemoglobin level less well tolerated.
pitfalls: Misreading a normal-appearing enzyme level that is falsely raised by reticulocytosis
Overlooking the low 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate and its effect on oxygen delivery
Assuming a membrane disorder when spherocytes are absent
Neglecting iron-overload monitoring in transfused patients
management: No specific therapy exists; provide supportive care with folic acid supplementation and red cell transfusion for symptomatic anaemia, particularly in the neonatal period and infancy
Manage neonatal jaundice with phototherapy and, where severe, exchange transfusion
Monitor iron status and treat iron overload with chelation therapy in transfusion-dependent patients, avoiding unnecessary iron supplementation

Recognise that the characteristically low red-cell 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate shifts the oxygen dissociation curve, so a given haemoglobin may be less well tolerated and transfusion thresholds adjusted accordingly
Consider splenectomy in selected severe transfusion-dependent disease, with prior vaccination against encapsulated organisms and antibiotic prophylaxis
Offer genetic counselling and family testing given autosomal recessive inheritance of HK1 variants, noting possible multisystem features
Provide ongoing haematology follow-up of haemoglobin, reticulocytes and haemolysis markers
